aboutParagraph: A glossary of Minecraft speedrunning terms, strategies, tools, and community language.

terms.name: All Advancements
terms.definition: All Advancements, usually shortened to AA, is the Java category whose objective is to earn every advancement required by the selected version group. Current rules finish on the chat notification for the last advancement and require proof that the full set was completed. Because Minecraft adds and changes advancements between releases, AA routes and leaderboard comparisons are version-specific; older version ranges may represent the corresponding achievements-era completion category under the consolidated board.

terms.name: Any%
terms.definition: **Any%** is the speedrun objective of reaching Minecraft’s defined ending as quickly as the category rules allow, without having to complete optional content or collect a percentage of the game. On the Minecraft: Java Edition leaderboard, `Any%` and `Any% Glitchless` are separate category names: the unqualified `Any%` board permits category-defined glitches, while RSG and SSG runs under glitchless rules sit under Any% Glitchless. Seed type, version range, and rule set therefore have to be stated separately. Under current Java Any% Glitchless rules, timing ends when the player enters an End exit portal and the credits begin, not merely when the dragon dies.

terms.name: Atum
terms.definition: **Atum** is a client-side Minecraft: Java Edition reset mod used to start repeated Random Seed or Set Seed attempts without navigating the normal world-creation menus each time. In reset mode, leaving a world or pressing its reset hotkey starts another world using the configured seed and world settings. Modern 1.16.1 setups often use Atum together with WorldPreview, FastReset, or SeedQueue; those tools accelerate other parts of resetting and do not change Atum’s basic job. Only builds on the current official legal-mod list are valid for speedrun.com submissions.

terms.name: Axis Calculated
terms.definition:
**Axis Calculated** is a legacy sheet-based method for locating a stronghold during Java 1.16 RSG. After the first Nether exit, the runner makes two Eye of Ender measurements from carefully chosen positions near chunk boundaries, records the eye's major and minor directions and its angle change, then combines those readings with the first portal's coordinates in the Axis Calculated sheet. The result is a target for a second Nether portal near the stronghold.

Axis Calculated is a specific form of Calculated Travel, usually used as part of a 20-obsidian Double Travel route. Stronghold calculators made the original workflow much less common after they became legal in December 2021, but the method remains legal and is still relevant to no-calculator play.
terms.historicalNote: Legacy Java 1.16 RSG sheet workflow; legal calculators sharply reduced its competitive use after December 2021.

terms.name: Bastion
terms.definition: A **bastion** is the MCSR community’s usual name for a Bastion Remnant, a large Nether structure containing piglins, gold, and layout-specific chests. In Java 1.16.1 Any% RSG and MCSR Ranked, runners route a bastion so they can barter its gold with several piglins at once, chiefly seeking ender pearls, obsidian, string, and Fire Resistance. Bastions generate in four layouts—Bridge, Housing, Stables, and Treasure—and each supports different routes. Bastions also exist after 1.16.1, but piglin brutes and later barter tables change their risk and routing, so 1.16.1 instructions are not automatically valid for newer versions.

terms.name: Bastion Route
terms.definition: A **bastion route** is a practiced path and piglin setup for a particular Bastion Remnant layout. The route coordinates chest and gold collection, lures or moves piglins into a trading hole, and uses the bartering time for inventory management or other run preparation. Bridge, Housing, Stables, and Treasure each have their own route families, and the right choice can change with the entrance, rampart generation, terrain or lava, available blocks, and the resources already in the runner’s inventory. Most named routes discussed in modern RSG and Ranked guides are for Java 1.16.1; they should not be assumed safe or optimal in versions with piglin brutes.

terms.name: Blaze
terms.definition: A **blaze** is the Nether Fortress mob runners kill to obtain blaze rods for Eyes of Ender. Runners normally use a fortress blaze spawner because it provides repeated spawn attempts in a known area, then leave once their rod supply is sufficient for the run’s remaining eyes. In vanilla Java Edition, a blaze killed by a player has a 50% chance to drop one rod without Looting. MCSR Ranked separately standardizes blaze-rod outcomes and spawner timing and positions so both competitors receive matching RNG; those are Ranked rules, not vanilla blaze behavior.

terms.name: Blaze Bed

media.title: Practical Guide to Blaze Bedding in Minecraft Speedrunning
media.caption: Open and enclosed Blaze Bed setups

terms.name: Blaze Rods
terms.definition: **Blaze rods** are the fortress-stage resource runners obtain from blazes. Each rod can be crafted into two blaze powder, and each powder combines with an ender pearl to make one Eye of Ender for locating and activating a stronghold’s End portal. In vanilla Java Edition, a qualifying blaze kill drops one rod half the time without Looting; MCSR Ranked instead standardizes the competitors’ blaze-rod sequence. Runners choose how many rods to collect from the eyes already in the portal, possible eye breaks, spare pearls, and the amount of risk they are willing to take, so there is no single rod count built into the term.

terms.name: Blaze TNT
terms.definition: **Blaze TNT** is a Java 1.16.1 fortress technique that uses a planned TNT explosion to clear blocks around a blaze spawner. Removing obstructions reduces blocked spawn positions and makes blazes easier to see and fight while collecting rods. It serves the same broad purpose as Blaze Bed, but the item and placements differ; a bad setup can destroy the spawner, so runners learn fixed layouts for common terrain configurations.

terms.name: Blind Travel

media.title: Minecraft Nether Travel – An Introduction to Blind Travel and Educated Travel
media.caption: Blind Travel explained and demonstrated

terms.name: Boat Eye
terms.definition:
**Boat Eye** is a current high-precision Eye of Ender measurement technique used with Ninjabrain Bot. Entering and exiting a boat puts the player's view angle into a predictable state; after the runner gives that boat angle to the bot, the bot can recover more precision than the two decimal places supplied by F3+C. The runner then measures the thrown eye with precise pixel corrections.

A correct Boat Eye measurement can often give the calculator a high-confidence stronghold target from one eye, saving the time and movement needed for an ordinary second measurement. It is used in modern Java 1.16 RSG and Ranked, although newer sensitivity setups may preserve the required angle state without placing a boat immediately before every throw.

terms.name: Bridge Bastion

media.title: 2 Minute Bastions: Bridge
media.caption: Bridge Bastion structure overview

terms.name: Buried Treasure
terms.definition: Buried Treasure, usually shortened to **BT**, is a hidden single-chest structure and a common overworld start in Java 1.16.1 speedrunning. Its chest can supply early iron, cooked fish, gold, and other useful loot, letting a runner prepare for a nearby ocean or magma-ravine Nether entry without routing a village. Runners often locate it with the version-sensitive Mapless technique rather than a treasure map. In MCSR Ranked, Buried Treasure is also a filtered seed type with guaranteed resources and nearby entry options; those guarantees do not apply to ordinary RSG seeds.

terms.name: Calculated Travel
terms.definition: Calculated Travel is a legacy Java 1.16 RSG double-travel technique for estimating both the direction and distance to a stronghold without a modern stronghold bot. The runner exits the Nether through a first portal, measures two Eye of Ender throws, estimates the stronghold's Overworld position, then returns to the Nether and builds a second portal near the corresponding one-eighth-scale coordinates. It is more informed than Educated Travel, which uses direction without a calculated distance. Current rules permit stronghold calculators, while manual calculated methods remain useful to no-calculator runners.
terms.historicalNote: Pre-calculator 1.16 RSG travel method; still understood and used in no-calculator play.

terms.name: Classic
terms.definition: **Classic** is MCSR shorthand for completing a 1.16 route without entering a bastion. Traditional classic strats mine Nether gold and barter with ordinary piglins for pearls and other supplies, usually accepting lower consistency than a routed bastion in exchange for simpler execution or to salvage a seed. The route is legacy in modern RSG, but the term remains current: MCSR Ranked awards the `Classic` achievement for winning a completed match without entering a bastion.

terms.name: Completable Ruined Portal
terms.definition: A **Completable Ruined Portal**, often shortened to **Completable RP**, is a ruined portal that a runner can quickly repair and light using its existing regular obsidian and resources available at or near the structure. Chest obsidian or fire items, nearby lava, and the placement of crying obsidian determine whether the entry is practical. It is an important Java 1.16+ seed-evaluation term, especially in 1.16.1 RSG and Ranked; it describes a useful condition of a ruined portal, not a separate vanilla structure type.

terms.name: Desert Temple
terms.definition: A **Desert Temple**, officially called a Desert Pyramid and often shortened to **DT**, is a desert structure with four loot chests above a nine-TNT pressure-plate trap. Speedrunners drop beside the plate, disable it, and route whichever chest loot or TNT the category makes useful. Desert Temples are situational in ordinary RSG because the loot may not support a fast Nether entry, but MCSR Ranked treats them as a filtered seed type with guaranteed minimum iron, food, and nearby lava access. Those filter guarantees are not vanilla behavior.

terms.name: Divine Travel
terms.historicalNote: Top-level 1.16.1 RSG runs used this technique in 2021; it remains legal and tool-supported but niche.

media.title: How to Divine Travel in Minecraft Speedrunning
media.caption: Divine Travel conditions and fossil setup

terms.name: Donkey Kong Route
terms.definition: The **Donkey Kong Route**, usually shortened to **DK**, is a current Java 1.16.1 route family for Bridge Bastions. It uses the bastion's chalice gold and funnels piglins gathered from the bridge and ramparts into a controlled trading position. Left- and right-side DK variants handle different rampart and chest generations, so the name describes a family of Bridge routes rather than one universal block-for-block path.

terms.name: Double Travel
terms.definition:
**Double Travel** is a Java 1.16 RSG and Ranked route that uses two Nether-to-Overworld exits to approach the stronghold. The runner builds a first exit, measures one or more Eyes of Ender in the Overworld, returns through that portal, travels toward the estimated stronghold position in the Nether, and builds a second exit near the target. Because horizontal distance is scaled 1:8 between the Nether and Overworld, the second Nether leg can replace a much longer Overworld journey.

The standard route needs 20 obsidian for two complete portal frames, which is why runners often use “20 obsidian” as a route decision. Double Travel describes the portal plan, not the calculation itself: Axis Calculated, Perfect Travel, ordinary triangulation, or Ninjabrain Bot can be used to choose the second portal's coordinates.

terms.name: Educated Travel
terms.historicalNote: Pre-calculator direction-only 1.16 travel term; still used in no-calculator discussion.

media.title: Minecraft Nether Travel – An Introduction to Blind Travel and Educated Travel
media.caption: Educated Travel explained

terms.name: Elo
terms.definition: **Elo** is MCSR Ranked's name for the numerical rating used to order its competitive ladder and help match players of similar strength. After placement matches, winning normally raises a player's Elo and losing lowers it; the amount depends in part on the opponent's rating. Elo belongs to Ranked competition rather than to a Minecraft speedrun category. At season end, players become unranked and must complete placement matches again; current rank thresholds and decay rules should be checked against the live service documentation.

terms.name: End Entry
terms.definition: **End Entry** is the split at which a runner goes through an activated End portal and enters the End dimension. Runners quote the time—such as “a 7:51 end entry”—to describe the pace reaching the dragon fight, and Ranked/Paceman tools record the same milestone as a timeline event. End Entry is not the Any% Glitchless finish: the run continues through the dragon fight and ends at the ruleset's required credits transition.

terms.name: Ender Pearl
terms.definition: An **Ender Pearl**, usually just a **pearl**, is a throwable item that teleports the runner to its landing point and is also the Ender-Pearl half of an Eye of Ender recipe. Pearls are both progression resources and movement tools: runners spend them to cross Nether terrain, reach structures, recover movement, and get from the End spawn platform toward the dragon-fight setup. In Java 1.16.1 RSG and Ranked, bastion routes commonly source pearls through piglin bartering; that high-yield barter is version-specific and should not be assumed for later Minecraft versions.

terms.name: Eye of Ender
terms.definition: An **Eye of Ender**, usually shortened to an **eye**, is crafted from one Ender Pearl and one Blaze Powder. A thrown eye travels toward the nearest stronghold and may shatter, so runners measure its direction for navigation, triangulation, or a stronghold calculator while limiting unnecessary throws. Eyes also fill the twelve End portal frames, although individual frames can generate already filled. Java-specific techniques use the eye's relationship to the stronghold starter-staircase chunk; those chunk details should not be assumed to work the same way in Bedrock Edition.

terms.name: F3
terms.definition: F3 is MCSR shorthand for Minecraft: Java Edition’s debug screen and, in leaderboard rules, for any run that uses the screen or an F3-triggered feature. Runners read coordinates, facing, chunk position, entity counts and the Shift+F3 profiler to support navigation and techniques such as eye measurement, E-raying and pie-ray; shortcuts such as F3+B hitboxes also count as F3 under current Java rules. The available information and legal keybinding behavior vary by game version and ruleset.

terms.name: Filtered Seed
terms.definition: A filtered seed is a world seed selected by software because it meets a declared set of conditions, rather than an arbitrary seed accepted sight unseen. MCSR Ranked and FSG both use filtered seeds, but their filters and guarantees are different. Ranked currently filters the Overworld and Nether independently and uses filtered seeds in Ranked and Casual matches; FSG categories define their own filters and verification rules. The phrase alone therefore does not promise a particular start, structure distance or loot result.

terms.name: Flintless Portal
terms.definition: A Flintless Portal is a Nether portal lit without flint and steel, usually by placing a flammable block beside a completed frame and using nearby lava to make fire spread into the portal opening. In Java 1.16 RSG it is a backup for an entry that has enough iron for the essential tools but no spare iron or flint for a normal light. The fire-spread wait is variable, and a runner who enters flintless still needs a plan to light the later Nether-side portal, such as obtaining a fire charge or making flint and steel.

terms.name: Forced Perch
terms.definition: Forced Perch is a historical MCSR Ranked term for the former safeguard that made the Ender Dragon begin perching after 2 minutes 50 seconds of in-game time from its spawn or previous perch. Ranked removed that fixed timeout in May 2026 when it introduced seed-standardized strafe and perch rolls; the current system instead guarantees a successful roll once the documented no-perch probability falls below 0.1. The old term should not be used as the name of the current system.
terms.historicalNote: Former MCSR Ranked 2:50 safeguard, removed in May 2026; current Ranked uses seed-standardized perch rolls instead.

terms.name: Fortress Navigation

media.title: Minecraft Speedrunners Guide to Navigating the Nether Fortress
media.caption: Fortress structure cues and spawner navigation

terms.name: FSG
terms.definition: FSG means Filtered Seed Glitchless, the Java speedrunning category family in which an approved filter supplies an unknown seed that meets that category’s declared conditions. It differs from RSG because the possible seeds are deliberately constrained, and from SSG because the runner is not repeatedly practicing one known world. Current FSG includes multiple filters, such as ZigSeedGlitchless and Seedbank, with their own guarantees and verification requirements; MCSR Ranked uses a separate filtered-seed system and is not itself FSG.

terms.name: Glitchless
terms.definition: Glitchless is an MCSR ruleset and category label, not a claim that every bug-like or unintended interaction is forbidden. The current Java rules allow only the glitches they list for Glitchless runs and prohibit other glitches, with moderators deciding borderline cases between a glitch and a technique. It combines with an objective and seed type in names such as Any% Random Seed Glitchless, so the current rules—not the everyday meaning of “glitchless”—determine whether a strategy is legal.

terms.name: Half Bow
terms.definition: Half Bow is an End-fight strategy in which a runner quickly shoots several End crystals, then stops and waits to one-cycle the dragon when it perches. In Java, each holding-pattern perch roll has a `1 / (3 + live crystals)` chance, so destroying crystals improves the odds on later rolls; runners usually leave caged or inconvenient towers rather than clear all ten. Shooting costs time and crystal breaks can send the dragon into a strafe, so Half Bow trades the fastest possible natural perch for a more consistent wait. That tradeoff makes the strategy useful in Ranked and other consistency-focused play.

terms.name: Housing Bastion

media.title: 2 Minute Bastions: Housing Units
media.caption: Housing Units structure overview

terms.name: Hypermodern
terms.definition: Hypermodern is a legacy 1.16 RSG label for the route family that minimized Overworld preparation and shifted essential resource collection into a bastion. Typical Hypermodern runs used an ocean or other fast Nether entry, then relied on bastion gold and piglin barters for pearls, string, obsidian and fire resistance before fortress play and blind travel. Community usage was loose: some runners meant ocean-start routes specifically, while others meant bastion-based play generally in contrast with Classic routes. The component strategies remain familiar, but the label is mainly useful for understanding the early 1.16 route-development era.
terms.historicalNote: Early-1.16 RSG route label; its bastion-first components remain familiar, but the umbrella term is now less common.

terms.name: IGT
terms.definition: IGT means **in-game time**, the official time measurement used by many Minecraft: Java Edition leaderboard categories. It removes only the periods excluded by that category's rules—such as specified loading, joining, pausing, or full-freeze intervals—rather than simply counting whatever an on-screen timer happens to show. Current Java submissions use SpeedRunIGT data where required, with manual retiming available when the automatic value is not usable, so the exact start, finish, and exclusions still come from the rules for the run being submitted.

terms.name: Lava Pool
terms.definition: A **lava pool**, also called a lava lake, is a naturally generated group of lava source blocks that a runner can use to cast a Nether portal. In RSG, a useful pool needs enough accessible source blocks and a workable place for water and the portal frame; runners weigh those conditions against the time needed to reach and build at it. It is one of several Nether-entry resources, alongside ocean ravines and completable ruined portals.

terms.name: Lava Pool Portal

media.title: Incredibly fast Nether Portal Build (in 8 seconds)
media.caption: Eight-second lava-pool portal build

terms.name: Leaderboard
terms.definition: A **leaderboard** is the ordered record of accepted runs for a particular game, category, and set of variables. On Minecraft: Java Edition's Speedrun.com board, runners submit the proof required by the current rules and moderators verify submissions before placement. Times from different seed types, versions, difficulties, or timing methods are separate comparisons, and a community-recognized run can exist without being accepted onto a specific board.

terms.name: LiveSplit
terms.definition: **LiveSplit** is a general-purpose speedrun timer that stores segment splits and compares an attempt against a personal best, best segments, or other saved runs. Minecraft runners commonly used it in older setups, and it remains useful for display and pace comparison, but modern Java RSG timing is normally captured by SpeedRunIGT instead. A LiveSplit display does not override the category's official timing or proof rules.
terms.historicalNote: Common in older Minecraft timing setups; modern Java RSG normally uses SpeedRunIGT for official in-game timing.

terms.name: Magma Ravine
terms.definition: A **magma ravine**, often called an ocean ravine, is the 1.16.1 ocean feature runners use for a submerged Nether entry. The magma blocks and bubble columns mark a ravine whose floor exposes lava beneath the water; with a bucket and suitable blocks, the runner casts a portal from that lava while managing air and water flow. This remains relevant to 1.16.1 RSG and Ranked routing, but later world-generation versions do not provide the same route.

terms.name: Mapless

media.title: How to Find Buried Treasure in 150 Seconds (Mapless, Map)
media.caption: Mapless buried-treasure finding across Java versions

terms.name: Matchmaking
terms.definition: **Matchmaking** is the MCSR Ranked system that pairs a queued player with one opponent for a race. Ranked uses Elo as its main pairing factor. The Accurate, Balanced, and Fast settings change the eligible Elo range; below 1500 Elo, similar forfeit rate is a secondary factor whose weight decreases as the queue continues. Casual uses a separate queue, and its Unlimited Casual Queue setting permits opponents of any Elo.

terms.name: MCSR Ranked
terms.definition: **MCSR Ranked** is a Java 1.16.1 Fabric mod and competitive platform for live Minecraft speedrun races. In its standard head-to-head modes, two players run separate worlds built from the same filtered seed, while selected randomness such as piglin trades and blaze drops is standardized so route choice and execution decide more of the match. Ranked play changes Elo; Casual, Private Rooms, and Weekly Race use the same platform for different competitive or practice formats.

terms.name: Microlensing

media.title: Original 2020 Guide to Bastion Xray/Microlensing in Minecraft Speedrunning 1.16
media.caption: Original 2020 bastion microlensing guide

terms.name: Minecraft Speedrunning
terms.definition: **Minecraft speedrunning**, commonly shortened to MCSR, is playing a defined Minecraft objective for the fastest valid time under a category's rules. Those objectives and rules vary: Java and Bedrock, random and set seed, different versions, All Advancements, category extensions, and competitive Ranked races are not interchangeable. In Java Any% Glitchless, for example, completion is reaching the End, defeating the dragon, and entering the exit portal, but that familiar route is only one part of MCSR.

terms.name: Multi-Instance
terms.definition: **Multi-instance** is a legacy RSG reset setup that keeps several separate Minecraft clients open so multiple seeds can generate and be inspected in parallel. It reduces the idle time between attempts, but demands more system resources and is subject to the official multi-instance recording and directory rules. Modern 1.16.1 runners are generally directed to SeedQueue, which generates concurrent worlds inside one Minecraft instance; multi-instancing remains legal and can still be used, especially on versions SeedQueue does not support.
terms.historicalNote: The official guide directs 1.16.1 runners to SeedQueue; multi-instancing remains legal and useful on other versions.

terms.name: Nether Entry
terms.definition: **Nether Entry** is the milestone—and usually the split time—when a run reaches the Nether. In 1.16.1 RSG and Ranked it marks the end of the opening Overworld work: evaluating the seed, collecting early resources, and building or completing a portal. Runners use “nether entry,” “enter Nether,” and “nether enter” when comparing openings and setting pace targets.

terms.name: Nether Exit
terms.definition: Nether Exit is the point in a run when the runner leaves the Nether and returns to the Overworld after the Nether resource segment. In Java 1.16.1 RSG and Ranked discussion, runners use the exit time as a major pace checkpoint because it follows bastion trading, blaze collection, and the choice of where to build or use the return portal. The exit is often a Blind Travel portal, but the terms are not interchangeable: Blind Travel describes a targeting strategy, while Nether Exit names the transition or split.

terms.name: Nether Fortress
terms.definition: A **Nether Fortress**, usually shortened to **fortress** or **fort**, is the Nether structure where Any% runners collect blaze rods for Eyes of Ender. Runners normally locate a blaze spawner, navigate to the fortress’s spawner side, and fight blazes until they have enough rods for the rest of their route. In modern 1.16.1 RSG and Ranked, the fortress is one of the two main Nether structures alongside a bastion, although either structure can be visited first.

terms.name: Nether Travel

media.caption: One Nether block corresponds to eight blocks of horizontal Overworld coordinates
media.alt: Overworld and Nether lanes showing an eight-to-one horizontal coordinate scale

terms.name: Ninjabrain Bot

media.title: Ninjabrain Bot Stronghold Calculator Tutorial for Minecraft Speedruns (100% EYE SPY)
media.caption: Ninjabrain Bot setup and eye-measurement guide

terms.name: No F3
terms.definition: No F3 is the Minecraft Java speedrun classification for an attempt completed without using the debug screen or any feature triggered by an F3 hotkey during the run. That restriction includes tools such as coordinates and facing, hitboxes, chunk borders and the profiler pie chart; persistent F3 toggles must also be disabled before the attempt. Because those tools support structure finding, angle measurement and combat, No F3 routing relies more heavily on visible terrain, game knowledge and non-debug methods. Speedrun.com records F3 and No F3 as a run variable across several categories and version ranges; showing F3 only after completion for required proof is separate from using it during the timed run.

terms.name: No Reset
terms.definition: No Reset is an informal MCSR format in which the runner commits to each generated random seed instead of abandoning slow starts or difficult routes. It emphasizes completion, backup knowledge, and improvisation rather than selecting only record-pace seeds. Individual challenges may add hardcore, streak, average-time, or seed-count rules, so No Reset describes the commitment to play the seed and is not one universal Speedrun.com category.

terms.name: Obsidian
terms.definition: **Obsidian**, commonly shortened to **obby** or **obi**, is the block used for Nether portal frames. A minimal new portal needs 10 regular obsidian, while routes that build two new portals generally need about 20. In 1.16.1 RSG and Ranked, runners usually collect it from bastion chests and piglin bartering, and may reserve another blast-resistant block for a one-cycle setup in the End. Crying obsidian can serve in some explosion setups but cannot replace regular obsidian in a Nether portal frame.

terms.name: One Cycle

media.title: How to One Cycle
media.caption: One Cycle setup and bed timing

terms.name: Pace
terms.definition: **Pace** describes how an attempt is progressing toward a time goal. A runner may call a run “PB pace,” “WR pace,” or “sub-15 pace” when its current split, route state, resources, and remaining time save make that finish plausible. Pace is a live judgment, not a guarantee: later RNG or execution can still change the outcome.

terms.name: PaceMan
terms.definition: PaceMan is an MCSR live pace tracker. With its tracker enabled, SpeedRunIGT events are sent to paceman.gg so viewers and communities can follow active runners, split times, completed runs, and pace statistics in real time. PaceMan is a discovery and statistics service rather than an official speedrun leaderboard or proof system; a tracked run is not automatically a verified submission.

terms.name: PB
terms.definition: **PB** means **personal best**: the fastest time a runner has completed under a particular category and rules context. A PB does not have to be submitted to a leaderboard; leaderboard verification is a separate claim.

terms.name: Pearl Hanging
terms.definition: Pearl Hanging is a Java 1.16.1 technique that throws an Ender Pearl into a chunk the runner deliberately unloads by lowering render distance or moving away. The pearl stops being processed while unloaded; loading the chunk later lets it land and teleport the runner back, so bastion routes can overlap travel, looting, or escape setup. It depends on singleplayer chunk loading and version behavior, so practice maps, multiplayer, or newer pearl chunk-loading changes can prevent the same setup.

terms.name: Perch

media.title: Speedrunners Guide to End Fights Part 1: Mechanics
media.caption: Dragon pathing phases and perch mechanics

terms.name: Perfect Travel
terms.definition:
**Perfect Travel** is a legacy calculated-travel method that uses an unusually precise Eye of Ender direction to narrow the stronghold to a small set of possible start chunks. The runner measures an eye after the first Nether exit, applies a subpixel correction, and uses a lookup sheet or PerfectTravelBot to turn the angle and measurement chunk into candidate chunk offsets. In the original Java 1.16 RSG route, the runner then returned to the Nether and built a second portal at the selected target; the method could also provide an Overworld dig-down target.

Perfect Travel became much less common after general stronghold calculators were legalized in December 2021. Its original resources remain legal, and its precise eye-measurement ideas carried into later calculator techniques.
terms.historicalNote: Pre-general-calculator precise-eye lookup workflow; legal but much less necessary after calculators were permitted in December 2021.

terms.name: Pie Chart
terms.definition: The **Pie Chart**, also called the **F3 Pie Chart**, is Minecraft Java Edition's debug profiler graph. MCSR runners inspect its entity and block-entity readings to support techniques for locating structures or structure components, including fortress Pie-Ray and Mapless buried treasure. In Java 1.16.1 the chart opens with `Shift+F3`; Mojang changed the shortcut to `F3+1` in 1.20.2. The profiler path and interpretation depend on the target and game version, so the chart itself should be distinguished from the Pie-Ray techniques built around it.

terms.name: Pie-Ray
terms.definition: **Pie-Ray**, also called **Piedar**, is using Java Edition's profiler Pie Chart to infer the presence or direction of a structure or structure component from changing profiler readings. In Java 1.16.1 fortress Pie-Ray, runners detect a blaze spawner and use render-distance and chunk-border changes to narrow its direction. Mapless buried treasure, Preemptive portal-room locating, and newer-version methods use different profiler paths or procedures, so Pie-Ray is a family of target- and version-specific techniques rather than one universal scan.

terms.name: Piglin Bartering
terms.definition: **Piglin Bartering**, usually shortened to **bartering**, is giving gold ingots to adult piglins in exchange for randomized items. In Java 1.16.1 RSG, runners commonly feed bastion gold to several piglins at once and collect Ender Pearls, obsidian, string, fire resistance, and other route supplies while continuing the bastion or fortress split. The pearl barter was reduced in Java 1.16.2, so 1.16.1 routing should not be generalized to every version. MCSR Ranked also modifies and synchronizes selected barter results for its competitive matches.

terms.name: Placement Match
terms.definition: A **Placement Match**, also called a **placement game** or simply a **placement**, is one of the opening MCSR Ranked matches used to estimate a player's Elo before their normal ladder rating is shown. Players become unranked again at the start of a new season and complete placements for a new rating. The live Ranked documentation says how far a player advances in each placement matters; exact counts and rating calculations are service rules that can change, so they should not be hard-coded into the glossary definition.

terms.name: Portal Room
terms.definition: The **Portal Room**, or **End Portal Room**, is the stronghold room containing the twelve-frame End portal above a lava pool and a silverfish spawner. Runners find it through stronghold navigation or a version-specific profiler technique, then place Eyes of Ender in every empty frame to activate the portal and enter the End. Individual frames can generate already filled, reducing the number of eyes needed at the room. Breaking the spawner is optional rather than part of the definition.

terms.name: Preemptive Navigation
terms.definition: Preemptive Navigation, usually shortened to preemptive or preemptive nav, is a Java 1.16.1 stronghold technique that uses the F3 profiler pie chart to detect the portal room's silverfish spawner and narrow down its direction before choosing a route. Runners rotate through narrow views and refresh the chart to isolate a block-entity spike, then combine that direction with normal room and branch navigation. The reading is not an exact coordinate or guaranteed path: chests, other spawners, mobs, chunk culling and render settings can distort it, so a runner may need to rescan or fall back to systematic stronghold navigation. The technique is current in RSG, FSG and MCSR Ranked, but it is not available in a No F3 run.

terms.name: Random Seed
terms.definition: **Random Seed**, often shortened to **RS**, is a speedrun seed ruleset in which the runner does not enter or choose the world seed in advance. The current Minecraft Java rules require the seed input to be left entirely blank, whether the world is created through vanilla menus or an approved reset tool. Random Seed describes seed selection only: an RS run can be glitched or glitchless and can have different objectives. **RSG** is the more specific abbreviation for Random Seed Glitchless.

terms.name: Reset
terms.definition: A **reset** is abandoning the current speedrun attempt and starting or selecting another world. In RSG, resetting is also seed evaluation: runners compare the world's visible start, available route, execution, and current pace with their goal, then decide whether continuing is worth more than rolling another attempt. Modern approved tools such as Atum and multi-instance setups make the transition faster, but automation and recording still have to follow the current category rules. Resetting is optional; stricter criteria make sense for record attempts than for a runner seeking practice or a first completion.

terms.name: Reset Efficiency
terms.definition: **Reset Efficiency** is how effectively an RSG runner turns real session time into promising attempts. It includes the technical speed of generating, previewing, and replacing worlds, plus the judgment to reject weak starts without discarding too many seeds that fit the runner's route and goal. Legal reset tools and the Wall can improve throughput, but route knowledge and seed-selection criteria are also part of the skill.

terms.name: RNG
terms.definition: **RNG** stands for **Random Number Generation** and is MCSR shorthand for the game's uncertain events or for the result of a particular random roll. World generation, piglin barters, mob drops, spawns, Eye of Ender breaks, and dragon behavior are common examples, although their exact logic differs by version and mechanic. Runners can manage risk with route choices and backup resources, but ordinary RSG keeps the game's random variance. MCSR Ranked separately standardizes a documented subset of RNG for matched competition.

terms.name: RNG Standardization
terms.definition: **RNG Standardization**, or **standardized RNG**, is MCSR Ranked's system for using an RNG Seed to give opponents matched result sequences for selected random events. The current system covers examples such as piglin barters, many mob and block drops, Eye of Ender breaks, spawner attempts, portal behavior, prefilled End-portal-frame counts, and several Ender Dragon rolls; some outcomes also have Ranked-specific guarantees or rates. It improves competitive comparability but does not remove all randomness or guarantee identical results when players take different actions or block different spawn attempts.

terms.name: RSG
terms.definition: **RSG** means **Random Seed Glitchless**: the runner leaves the seed input blank and follows the current glitchless rules for the chosen objective and version. The acronym does not itself mean Any% or Java 1.16.1, although bare `RSG` often refers to Java Any% Random Seed Glitchless in community conversation. Strategies vary by edition and version, and `glitchless` means the board's defined ruleset—not an assumption that every behavior someone might call a glitch is forbidden.

terms.name: RTA
terms.definition: **RTA** means **Real Time Attack**, usually shortened in prose to **real time**. It is the elapsed real-world clock time from a category's defined start to its finish, normally continuing through Minecraft loading screens and pauses that IGT excludes. The exact start, finish, and any segmentation exceptions come from the category rules. Many Minecraft Java leaderboards rank runs by IGT while also recording RTA, but some categories explicitly use RTA as their primary timing method.

terms.name: Ruined Portal
terms.definition: A Ruined Portal, often shortened to RP, is a naturally generated partial Nether portal that can provide a fast Overworld route in 1.16+ speedruns. Runners inspect its frame and nearby chest for regular obsidian and a way to light the portal; if the missing frame blocks can be supplied quickly, it is called a completable ruined portal. Crying obsidian does not work as part of an active frame, so some layouts require replacing it or cannot be completed efficiently. Even an unusable frame may offer gold, obsidian or a fire charge, but the structure and loot vary by seed.

terms.name: Seed
terms.definition: A seed is the input Minecraft uses to generate a world. Under the same edition, game version and relevant world settings, it reproduces the terrain and structure layout that runners route; changes to generation can make the same seed behave differently in another version. In MCSR, seed handling separates formats: Random Seed leaves the seed input blank, Set Seed deliberately supplies one, and filtered formats select seeds that meet declared conditions. A seed fixes world generation, not every barter, drop, mob action or other source of gameplay RNG.

terms.name: Seedbank
terms.definition: Seedbank is a current 1.16.1 FSG filter and leaderboard category built around seeds selected for a looting-sword ruined-portal start and favorable Nether and stronghold conditions. The name may refer to the filter, its pool of qualifying seeds, or the category where runs on those seeds are ranked. FSG Mod can issue a fresh Seedbank seed with a verification token from the online database; that seed is then removed from the unused competitive pool, while practice mode reuses past seeds and is not leaderboard-verifiable. The board was formerly called Seedbank/Legacy Filters, and older filter runs remain on it, so its historical results do not all represent one unchanged filter.

terms.name: SeedQueue
terms.definition: SeedQueue is a Minecraft speedrunning mod that generates several worlds concurrently inside one game instance and displays them on an in-game wall so a runner can discard or select previews quickly. It was designed as a lower-overhead replacement for traditional multi-instancing and is the current recommended reset system for Java 1.16.1 RSG. SeedQueue does not make seeds better or filtered by itself; filtered play requires a separate filter or client. Runs submitted to a leaderboard must use a currently legal build and follow its SeedQueue configuration and evidence rules.

terms.name: Set Seed
terms.definition: Set Seed, abbreviated SS, is a speedrun seed type in which the runner deliberately supplies a known seed before the attempt. Because the world layout can be scouted and replayed, runners can optimize exact movement, structures, crafting and backups for that seed. Set Seed does not by itself specify the goal or glitch rules: SSG means Set Seed Glitchless, while other Set Seed categories can have different objectives or rulesets. Current Java rules generally time Set Seed from first input, but the applicable category rules remain authoritative.

terms.name: Shipwreck
terms.definition: A Shipwreck, often shortened to Ship, is an ocean or beach structure used as an Overworld start in 1.13+ speedruns. Depending on which sections generated, it can contain a supply chest with food, a treasure chest with iron and other valuables, and a map chest leading to buried treasure; its planks and logs can also supply early wood. In 1.16.1 RSG and Ranked, runners quickly identify the ship’s orientation and surviving sections to decide which chests to loot and whether the seed has a practical Nether entry. Not every ship has all three chests or enough resources to justify continuing.

terms.name: Spawn
terms.definition: Spawn is the place and immediate starting situation where a player appears. In RSG and Ranked, runners judge an Overworld spawn by visible terrain, food, structures and Nether-entry options before deciding whether to play or reset; on a Set Seed route, the spawn is known and rehearsed. Runners also say Nether spawn or End spawn for the position reached on entering those dimensions. The word is therefore broader than Minecraft’s technical world-spawn point and should not be treated as an exact synonym for it.

terms.name: Speedrun.com
terms.definition: Speedrun.com, commonly shortened to SRC, is the platform that hosts the main community-run Minecraft leaderboards and run submissions. Its Minecraft pages organize times by objective, seed type, version and other variables, while community moderators review evidence and curate the boards. For Java Edition, the complete current rules are maintained by the Minecraft Java speedrunning organization on its rules site and repository, with an abridged version linked from SRC. MCSR Ranked is a separate head-to-head service and is not affiliated with speedrun.com.

terms.name: SpeedRunIGT
terms.definition: SpeedRunIGT is an open-source Minecraft: Java Edition timer mod that reads game events to start, pause and finish supported speedrun categories and can display both in-game time and real time. Current Java leaderboard rules use its reported value as the run’s IGT when the approved mod, correct category and required precision/evidence conditions are met. It supports many game versions, so runners must install a build currently legal for the version they run. `IGT` is the timing method; SpeedRunIGT is one specific tool that records it, and MCSR Ranked races use their own RTA timing.

terms.name: Split
terms.definition: A split is a timed checkpoint used to show how far an attempt has progressed, such as Nether entry, bastion entry, fortress, stronghold or End entry. Timer software usually records the split as the cumulative time at that checkpoint and calls the interval since the previous checkpoint a segment. MCSR runners also use `split` more loosely for the phase itself, as in `Nether split` or `end split`. Split layouts are chosen for practice and comparison rather than fixed by one official MCSR standard.

terms.name: SSG
terms.definition: SSG means Set Seed Glitchless: the runner deliberately supplies a known seed and follows the current Glitchless rules for the chosen objective and version. Repeating the same known world lets runners pre-route exact movement, structures, crafting, and backups, but SSG does not identify one route or version; leaderboards separate version ranges and objectives. It is narrower than Set Seed, which can also be used with non-glitchless rules.

terms.name: StandardSettings
terms.definition: **StandardSettings** is a Java speedrunning mod that reapplies a runner-chosen set of options whenever a world starts. It keeps settings such as render distance, FOV, difficulty, and configured debug behavior from carrying over unpredictably after an attempt. The mod does not choose a category-correct setup for the runner: its saved values must still match the current rules and the technique being used.

terms.name: Starter Staircase
terms.definition: The **starter staircase** is the first piece generated in a Java Edition stronghold and the reference point runners use for locating and navigating the structure. Stronghold calculations target its chunk, and the staircase's position and the adjacent five-way establish which doors and branches lead farther into the stronghold. Finding starter is therefore different from finding the portal room: it gives the runner a known origin from which to search.

terms.name: Stronghold
terms.definition: A **stronghold** is the Overworld structure that contains an End portal room. In Java Any% runs, locating the stronghold and finding its portal room are separate tasks: Eye of Ender measurements lead the runner to the starter staircase area, then stronghold navigation is used inside. After every empty frame receives an eye, the portal opens and the runner can enter the End.

terms.name: Village
terms.definition: A **village** is an Overworld structure that can supply several early-run needs in one place. In 1.16.1 routes, runners may take beds for the End fight, hay or other food, iron from the golem or smith chests, wood and workstations, then use that material to prepare a Nether entry. The biome, buildings, iron, food, villagers, and nearby lava determine whether a particular village is worth playing; faster target times often demand unusually strong village conditions.

terms.name: Wall
terms.definition: The **Wall** is an RSG reset interface that displays several generating or loaded world previews together so a runner can discard weak seeds, lock promising ones, and choose the next attempt. Older Walls used multiple separate Minecraft clients, while modern Java 1.16.1 setups commonly use SeedQueue's wall screen inside one instance. The Wall improves preview and selection throughput but does not filter or make vanilla seeds better by itself.

terms.name: WorldPreview
terms.definition: **WorldPreview** is a Java speedrunning mod that renders already generated chunks on the world-loading screen. It lets a runner evaluate and reject a seed before normal world entry, and works with reset systems such as SeedQueue or multi-instance walls to reduce time spent waiting on unplayable starts. The preview does not alter generation, but leaderboard runs must satisfy the current recording and interaction rules for the exact approved version.

terms.name: WR
terms.definition: **WR** means **world record**: the fastest recognized valid result for a specific category and its variables at a given time. In Minecraft, edition, seed type, version range, difficulty, F3 rules, mods, and timing method can separate records that look superficially similar. `WR` is also used for extension formats such as FSG, so the category and governing board should accompany the claim.

terms.name: ZSG
terms.definition: ZSG, short for ZigSeedGlitchless, is a current 1.16.1 FSG filter family and leaderboard category built to provide strong, RSG-like seeds. The filter selects worlds with favorable Overworld and Nether conditions, but runners still have to route and execute the resulting seed normally; regular variants are intended for realistic practice, while OP variants use more generous conditions. ZSG now includes several possible Overworld start filters, so it does not always mean a buried-treasure seed. It is commonly used to practice decision making on good seeds, but a ZSG run belongs to the FSG category rather than unfiltered RSG or MCSR Ranked.
